title: Apparent Zero-Momentum Signals from Magnon--Magnon Interference in Near-Field Spin-Wave Imaging
authors: Julien Berthomier, Romain Lebrun, Vincent Cros, Jamal Ben Youssef, Karim Bouzehouane, Abdelmadjid Anane
abstract: Spatially resolved measurements of coherent waves are commonly read as direct maps of the underlying eigenmode spectrum. We show that this interpretation fails in near-field imaging of multimode spin-wave transport. Scanning nitrogen-vacancy magnetometry of yttrium iron garnet reveals pronounced apparent low-wave-vector signals at frequencies for which no propagating spin-wave mode exists. By tuning the probe-sample distance and modeling the anisotropic near-field response, we identify their origin as coherent mixing between directly excited Damon-Eshbach waves and defect- or transducer-scattered spin waves: the measured signal acquires spatial Fourier components at the difference wave vector $\mathbf{k}_{\mathrm{exc}}-\mathbf{k}_{\mathrm{scat}}$, which can vanish even though both constituent waves carry finite momentum. These results establish that near-field spectra of coherent excitations are interferometric field spectra rather than eigenmode maps, providing both a caution and a framework for identifying scattering processes in nanoscale magnonic devices.
summary: This research demonstrates that near-field imaging of spin waves does not directly map the material's eigenmode spectrum. By analyzing signals from YIG films, the authors show that apparent low-momentum signals are actually due to coherent interference between different spin-wave components. This establishes that such measurements yield an interferometric field spectrum rather than a simple eigenmode map.
main_problem: The standard interpretation that spatially resolved measurements of coherent waves directly map the underlying eigenmode spectrum fails when imaging multimode spin-wave transport in the near-field.
main_result: The observed low-momentum signals are not true eigenmodes but are instead artifacts arising from the coherent interference (beating) between directly excited spin waves and those scattered by defects or sample imperfections.
method: The study combines experimental measurements using scanning nitrogen-vacancy magnetometry with theoretical modeling based on the Near-Field Diffraction (NFD) framework to decompose the total measured field.
model_or_system: The physical system is spin-wave propagation in a yttrium iron garnet (YIG) film. The analysis models the total local microwave field as a superposition of contributions from the antenna, the primary excited spin waves, and scattered spin waves.
key_observables: The total local microwave field $B_{tot}(\mathbf{r})$ and its spatial Fourier components, particularly the anomalous components appearing at the difference wave vector $\Delta \mathbf{k} = \mathbf{k}_{exc} - \mathbf{k}_{scat}$.
important_parameters: Probe-sample distance ($d$), wave vectors ($\mathbf{k}_{exc}, \mathbf{k}_{scat}$), and the relative strength of the interference term compared to the primary excitation fields.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the NFD model and assumes that the measured signal is dominated by the coherent interference cross-term when analyzing the anomalous signals.
figures_summary: Figures compare experimental contrast maps at different distances ($d=200$ nm vs $d=50$ nm) and show that the anomalous low-$k$ signal is reproduced by the theoretical cross-term ($\mathbf{B}_{SW,exc}\mathbf{B}_{SW,scat}$) in the NFD simulations.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the failure of the direct eigenmode mapping assumption, presents experimental evidence of anomalous low-$k$ signals, and then uses the NFD model to theoretically identify the origin of these signals as magnon-magnon interference terms.
why_interesting: This work provides a crucial methodological caution for experimental condensed matter physicists studying wave phenomena, showing that advanced near-field techniques require careful deconvolution of interference effects from true material properties.
